terms.gloss: I appreciate it, it is welcome to me
terms.grammar: phrase: the thing appreciated is the subject, or follows in a quod-clause; the person in the dative
evidence: Plin. Ep. 4.1.1: grātum est utrīque nostrum quod cupis
Cic. Fam. 2.18.1: tibi … grāta esse vehementer gaudeō
terms.comment: Latin turns the sentence round: what I appreciate is grātum, welcome, to me. Stronger: pergrātum, grātissimum.

terms.gloss: do something one appreciates; I’d appreciate it if you …
terms.grammar: phrase: the person in the dative; the polite request in the future perfect with sī
evidence: Cic. Fam. 2.19.2: grātissimum mihi fēceris, sī ad mē in Ciliciam quam prīmum vēneris
Cic. Att. 9.7.2: pergrātumque mihi tū fēcistī
terms.comment: The courteous formula of Cicero’s letters: grātum mihi fēceris, sī …, “I’d appreciate it if …”; after the event, grātum mihi fēcistī, “I appreciate what you did”.

terms.gloss: thank you, I appreciate it (for a kindness done)
terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.; Cic. in epistulīs
evidence: Plaut. Poen. 1.2.40: ergō amō tē, I like you, am much obliged to you (Lewis & Short s.v. amō)
Ter. Ad. 5.8.23: bene facis: meritō tē amō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The thanks of conversation (see thank you).
Tuērī is to look after, protect, keep up (Lewis & Short), so the phrase says “I am looking after your kindness”. Say grātum mihi est or Amō tē (above).

phrases.latin: quās sī satis opportūnō tempore accēpistī, grātissimum mihi fēceris, sī ad mē in Ciliciam quam prīmum vēneris.
phrases.english: if you have received it in good time, I’d very much appreciate it if you came to me in Cilicia as soon as possible.

phrases.latin: cupis post longum tempus neptem tuam mēque ūnā vidēre. grātum est utrīque nostrum quod cupis, mūtuō mehercule
phrases.english: you want to see your granddaughter, and me with her, after so long. We both appreciate that you want it, and, I promise, we feel the same

phrases.latin: Amō tē, et nōn neglēxisse habeō grātiam.
phrases.english: Thank you, and I appreciate your not forgetting.

sources: Cicero’s letters and Terence checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026). Pliny from the Latinitas loci collection loci-plinius, checked against the edition named there.
